title: Why flying can make you feel rough
description:
Ever wondered why you might feel a bit unwell after a flight? There are lots of reasons for that - from dehydration, jet lag, cabin pressure and altitude.

Last month, a French court recognised that cosmic radiation was a factor in a flight attendant’s breast cancer diagnosis. Studies show that cabin crew and pilots have the highest level of radiation- related cancer deaths compared to more than 500 other jobs.

We’re looking at what impacts flying regularly, and for long periods of time, can have on your body. We hear from Savannah, a pilot in the US, about what she does to keep herself healthy when sitting in a cockpit for hours. And Naomi, who is taking a break from being cabin crew, tells us how spending so much time in a plane has affected her.

summaryEn: In this episode of What in the World, host Hannah Gelbart explores why flying can physically impact the body, particularly for pilots and cabin crew who fly frequently. Cabin crew member Naomi and pilot Savannah share their experiences with severe dehydration, swollen legs, sleep deprivation, and exposure to UV rays at high altitudes. BBC Health Editor Michelle Roberts explains the science behind these symptoms, noting how low cabin pressure and dry air cause headaches, bloating, and poor blood circulation. She also discusses the risks of cosmic radiation for long-haul flight workers, while offering practical health advice for travelers, such as staying hydrated, applying sunscreen, getting adequate rest, and moving during flights.
